title: Traffic Mirroring End-to-End Benchmark Protocol
author: Priya N. Shah
body:
Summary

This document defines the canonical end-to-end (E2E) benchmark protocol for measuring runtime performance using traffic mirroring. Traffic mirroring benchmarks run real production traffic in read-only mode against candidate runtime builds, model variants, or kernel scheduling configurations. The goals are to:

- Obtain representative latency and correctness signals with minimal production risk.
- Compare candidate changes to a baseline across cost and tail-latency envelopes.
- Produce reproducible artifacts suitable for release gating and perf regression detection.

Scope

Applies to: eng-serving-runtime teams running hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. This protocol is intended for:
- New kernel scheduling releases
- Runtime build changes that touch request routing or batching
- Model-variant rollout validation (e.g., quantized vs float variants)
- Autoscaling/slotting policy experiments

Excludes: experiments that mutate customer-visible state or alter traffic semantics (see safety checklist).

Key Concepts

- Mirrored traffic: a copy of production requests sent concurrently to the candidate system without forwarding responses back to the user.
- Shadow target: an isolated cluster or pool that processes mirrored traffic for measurement and logging.
- Replay-safe: traffic transformed to remove sensitive PII and non-idempotent operations.

Roles and Ownership

- Benchmark Owner: person who schedules and signs off the run (example: Priya Shah).
- Runtime Owner: service-level owner of the candidate runtime build.
- Observability Owner: responsible for ensuring required dashboards and traces are available.
- SRE Approval: SRE must sign off for any run that exceeds baseline resource consumption thresholds.

SLOs and Acceptance Criteria

Baseline: production cluster A (stable). Candidate: cluster B (mirrored). Acceptance requires:
- P50 latency delta <= +10% compared to baseline under same load shape.
- P95 latency delta <= +15%.
- P99 tail-latency delta <= +25% OR absolute p99 < 3000ms (whichever is stricter for the workload).
- Throughput: candidate must sustain 95% of baseline sustained QPS without queue growth.
- Error rate (5xx): candidate <= baseline + 0.1 percentage points.
- Semantic parity: for deterministic workloads, token-level equality >= 98%. For non-deterministic outputs, use embed-similarity thresholds (cosine >= 0.985).

Safety Checklist (must be completed before any mirror run)

1) Sanitize inputs: remove Authorization headers and any customer PII using the request-sanitizer pipeline.
2) Ensure the candidate is strictly read-only: no upstream writes, no metrics emitted to billing systems.
3) Mirror traffic rate scaling: start at 1% of production QPS and increase only after SRE approval.
4) Resource isolation: shadow target must have separate autoscaling group / node-pool and no shared persistent storage with prod.
5) Alerting: create temporary alert suppressions to avoid noisy page storms and ensure critical alerts still page.

Procedure: Run Plan

1) Prepare candidate build and environment:
   - Deploy candidate runtime to shadow cluster B with identical network topology and model pins.
   - Ensure KV cache behavior is reset unless intentionally testing cache warmup.
   - Tag build with bench-run/<YYYYMMDD>/<run-id> for trace correlation.

2) Configure mirroring:
   - Use the traffic-mirror service (internal) to configure rule: mirror-rule:<service>-<route>-<run-id>.
   - Example rule config (YAML):

     mirror_rule: 
       name: chat-completions-shadow-2027-01
       source: prod-gateway
       match: path_prefix: "/v1/chat/completions"
       sampler: fixed_rate
       rate: 0.01
       sanitizer: request-sanitizer-v2
       targets: ["shadow-cluster-b"]

   - CLI to apply (internal):
     $ traffic-mirror apply --from prod-gateway --to shadow-cluster-b --path-prefix /v1/chat/completions --rate 0.01 --sanitizer request-sanitizer-v2 --name chat-completions-shadow-<run-id>

3) Warmup and ramping:
   - Start with 0.1% mirror rate for 10 minutes to validate pipeline. Confirm no errors and resource headroom.
   - Ramp to target mirror rate (commonly 1% or 5% depending on risk classification) in exponentially increasing steps (0.5%, 1%, 2%). Each step: hold for 5–15 minutes and observe metrics.

4) Data collection windows:
   - Short-run benchmarking: 30–60 minutes. Use when kernel or kernel-parameter changes are small.
   - Long-run benchmarking: 6–24 hours. Use for model-variant comparisons or autoscaling policy changes.
   - Capture request/response timeline traces, kernel metrics, GPU utilization, per-token latency histograms, KV cache hit rates, and queue length series.

5) Instrumentation and required telemetry

Required traces/metrics (minimum):
- request.timeline: trace spans for gateway->router->runtime->kernel->executor
- runtime.latency_ms: p50/p95/p99 histograms by route and model
- kernel.queue_length: 1s resolution time-series per GPU slot
- kernel.dispatch_time_ms: per-request quantiles
- gpu.utilization_pct: per-GPU
- kvcache.hit_rate: rolling 1m and 5m
- embed-similarity: sample of 200 request pairs comparing baseline vs candidate outputs

Tagging: all metrics must include bench.run_id and bench.build_tag dimensions.

Artifacts to persist

- Raw traces: stored in obs.test-bench/traces/<run-id> (retention 90d)
- Aggregated histograms: obs.test-bench/histograms/<run-id>.json
- Representative sample of requests and candidate responses (sanitized): s3://bench-artifacts/<run-id>/samples.jsonl.gz
- Perf report: s3://bench-artifacts/<run-id>/report.html (generated by bench-reporting tool)

Analysis and Reporting

1) Automated report generation:
   - After the run finishes the bench-orchestrator will produce a summary report containing latency deltas, resource deltas (GPU-hours used), and semantic similarity.
   - The report includes waterfall diagnostics for slow tail requests and a heatmap of queue growth over time.

2) Manual triage checklist:
   - If p99 delta > acceptance, run failure mode triage: inspect kernel dispatch traces, check for blocking allocations, and examine kernel-runloop starvation.
   - Compare kvcache.hit_rate trends: a sudden drop suggests cache population mismatch or differing shard keys.
   - Check for dispatcher backpressure events and kernel preemption counts.

3) Release gating:
   - Candidate passes if all acceptance criteria are met and no new critical incidents were generated during the run.
   - For marginal cases, run a focused replay of suspect requests with increased sampling (100–500x) to amplify differences for debugging.

Troubleshooting and Common Failure Modes

- Symptom: Elevated p95 with normal GPU utilization
  Action: Inspect kernel.queue_length and dispatch_time_ms for contention; verify batch-slicing thresholds and preemption windows.

- Symptom: Higher error rate on candidate
  Action: Check sanitizer pipeline for malformed transformed requests; validate model version pins; look for OOMs in runtime logs.

- Symptom: Semantic drift (embed-similarity drop)
  Action: Confirm identical tokenizer and model quantization parameters; check for off-by-one sequence padding differences.

- Symptom: Large cost delta with similar latency
  Action: Analyze per-token GPU cycles using kernel-cycle counters; check for degenerate scheduling producing small, inefficient kernels (e.g., repeated tiny-attention launches).

Operational Controls and Cost Limits

- Default mirror rate cap for non-critical patches: 1% of prod QPS.
- For kernel/platform team experiments that intentionally stress resources, a waiver must be obtained from SRE and Finance for temporary increased cloud spend (submit bench-cost-waiver/<run-id>).

Automation recipes and scripts

- bench-orchestrator job spec (short):
  - name: mirror-bench-<run-id>
  - baseline_cluster: prod-a
  - candidate_cluster: shadow-b
  - routes: ["/v1/chat/completions"]
  - mirror_rate: 0.01
  - sanitizer: request-sanitizer-v2
  - artifact_bucket: s3://bench-artifacts/<run-id>

- Example invocation:
  $ bench-orchestrator run --spec ./specs/mirror-bench-<run-id>.yaml --notify @eng-runtime --tag bench.run_id=<run-id>

Postmortem and Artifact Retention

- All run artifacts are retained for 90 days by default. Stakeholders must archive essential artifacts to the release retro bucket for multi-year retention if used for compliance.
- Any unexpected production-facing incident correlated to a mirroring run triggers a full incident review and possible rollback of mirror permissions.

Notes on Privacy and Compliance

- The request-sanitizer pipeline must run in-line before the mirror emitter. It should: strip auth tokens, normalize or redact PII fields, and replace customer ids with stable pseudonyms.
- For customers with restricted data residency, mirroring is disabled unless an explicit contractual exception is documented.

Appendix A: Example artifact schema (samples.jsonl line)

{
  "bench.run_id": "<run-id>",
  "timestamp": "2026-12-08T14:22:12Z",
  "route": "/v1/chat/completions",
  "sanitized_input": "{...}",
  "baseline_output_meta": {"latency_ms": 120, "tokens": 48},
  "candidate_output_meta": {"latency_ms": 160, "tokens": 48},
  "embed_similarity": 0.992
}

Appendix B: Quick checklist for small patch owners

1) Run preflight unit perf tests in sandbox.
2) Schedule 30min mirror at 0.5% and validate no increased error rate.
3) Expand to 1% for 60min and evaluate report.
4) If candidate is clean, request staging rollout.

- Bench-orchestrator docs: /tools/bench-orchestrator/guide
